I know. Another PDF API. Bear with me.
The problem I kept running into
Every time I needed HTML-to-PDF conversion in a project, I’d reach for one of the usual suspects: PDFShift, DocRaptor, API2PDF.
They all work. They’re all reasonably well documented.
PDFShift, for example, gives you 50 credits per month. Each credit covers a single conversion up to 5MB. If your document is larger — a report with charts, an invoice with logos, anything moderately complex — you burn multiple credits per test.
Before I’d finished validating my template, I was already thinking about upgrading to a paid plan I didn’t need yet.
That anxiety — “am I wasting test credits on this iteration?” — is exactly the wrong headspace to be in when you’re trying to build something.

articles.author: TwisterRL
articles.description:
[] == false        // true
[] == ![]          // true

Wait… what? 🤯
How can an empty array be equal to false?
JavaScript’s == operator performs type coercion.
That means it tries to convert values to the same type before comparing them.
[] == false

false becomes 0


[] becomes "" (empty string)
"" becomes 0



So we end up with:
0 == 0  // true

[] == ![]

First evaluate ![]:
[] is truthy
![] becomes false



So now we have:
[] == false

Which we already know is:
true

The == operator can lead to unexpected results because of implicit type conversion.
That’s why most developers prefer:
===

It compares values without coercion.
JavaScript doesn’t behave randomly.
Understand coercion, and the weirdness disappears.
Happy coding ✨
articles.title: JavaScript’s Weirdest Comparison

I used to think software versions are consecutive numbers which change after every update.  
Why does something go from v1.1 to v1.2?
The First Release


Imagine you and I build a simple app called TaskNest.
v1.0.0
Semantic Versioning. 
A Bug Appears


The next day, someone reports:
v1.0.1
v1.0.2
A Feature Grows


A week later, users ask:
v1.1.0
v1.2.0
The Big Decision


Months pass. The app grows.
v2.0.0
And That’s It
Last number → small fix
Middle number → new feature
First number → breaking change
It’s not random.
When you see v2.1.3, you’re not just seeing numbers.
“How much did I change the story?”
